HILO, Hawaii (AP) — Hurricane Nolo was gradually moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but some areas were still struggling to recover from earlier storms and continued to face threats from heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds.

As of Sunday morning, Nolo was located about 260 miles (415 kilometres) west-southwest of Hawaii's southernmost point, moving away from the Big Island at roughly 12 mph (19 kph). Even so, the Hawaii County Civil Defense Agency said that, with Nolo's top sustained winds having strengthened to near 105 mph (165 kph), high-wind warnings, wind advisories and high-surf advisories would remain in effect through Sunday evening, covering parts of the Big Island.

Nolo was forecast to intensify further and turn to the northwest by Sunday evening, though the National Hurricane Centre said the storm's centre would remain well to the south and southwest of the Hawaiian island chain. The storm was expected to approach the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument early in the week — a national conservation area.

Forecasters said its outer bands could bring life-threatening flash flooding and landslides, with rainfall totals on parts of the Big Island potentially reaching 20 inches (50 centimetres). Heavy rain was also forecast for other islands.

"Don't go outside unless you have to. We've got dangerous flooding conditions and strong winds. Trees could come down and power lines could fall at any moment," National Hurricane Centre director Michael Brennan said.

Heavy rain fell on the southern part of the Big Island on Saturday afternoon, forcing the partial closure of the main highway connecting Kailua-Kona on the west coast to Hilo on the east coast.

Near Naalehu, at the Big Island's southernmost tip, National Guard members guided a man through flooded streets during a downpour to help him leave his home. About 400 guardsmen across the state had been called up after the governor issued an emergency proclamation, with more than 120 stationed on the Big Island.

Residents had yet to recover from Hurricane Lala, whose heavy rain and strong winds were powerful enough to sweep roughly 100 homes on the Big Island completely off their foundations.

Hawaii braces as Nolo's northern edge looms

Despite posted beach closure signs, about a dozen people were in the water at Carlsmith Beach Park in Hilo on the Big Island on Saturday morning. Andrea Gill finished her usual swim and hurried home to brace for the storm with her family.

Businesses boarded up their storefronts, and numerous events were cancelled. Gill said storms were common locally, but hurricanes were rarer. She still held out hope that the archipelago might escape the worst.

"We're used to heavy rain, but not strong winds. Every time a hurricane comes through and doesn't bring strong winds, it's always something to be grateful for," Gill said.

President Donald Trump approved an emergency proclamation, authorising the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to coordinate disaster relief efforts and provide funding support.

Hawaiian Electric, the state's main utility, said repair crews who had earlier helped restore power on Kauai after Hurricane Lowell earlier in the month had returned to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island to prepare for Nolo.

Lead forecaster Bob Oravec at the National Weather Service said the Pacific had been unusually active this season, with storm activity during the peak of hurricane season still running above average. He noted this was consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific tends to produce more tropical storms and hurricanes.

Powerful Hurricane Polo forecast to track toward Mexico

Meanwhile, parts of Mexico's Baja California peninsula were bracing for the arrival of major Hurricane Polo. Polo was steadily approaching, having already brought heavy rain and strong winds to other stretches of the country's southwestern coast.

The U.S. National Hurricane Centre, based in Miami, said Sunday afternoon that Polo remained a dangerous Category 3 hurricane, with top sustained winds of 125 mph (205 kph), moving north-northwest at 12 mph (19 kph) while located about 285 miles (460 kilometres) southwest of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula's southern tip.

Mexico's national weather service, known by its Spanish abbreviation SMN, said in a post on the social platform X that Polo was expected to make landfall in Baja California on Monday.

The Mexican navy said in a statement that it had assembled personnel and humanitarian aid supplies at the Pacific coast ports of Guaymas and Mazatlan, and had dispatched three ships that could deliver supplies if the hurricane cut off coastal communities.

One town in the hurricane's forecast path is the small fishing village of San Juanico on Baja California's Pacific coast. The town only got round-the-clock electricity a few years ago and still loses power frequently. Locals worried that heavy rain could wash out roads, potentially preventing residents from reaching the nearest medical facility in Ciudad Constitucion, about an 80-minute drive away.

"Our residents are all worried about this. We haven't faced such a worrying situation in many years," said Gloriely Robles Meza, manager of a small local hotel.

Robles Meza said Sunday that the Mexican army had arrived in San Juanico to prepare shelters and provide support for any emergencies. An electrical repair crew had also been deployed to prepare for Polo's arrival.

Also on Sunday, the U.S. hurricane centre, headquartered in Miami, said Tropical Storm Rachel had formed far off Mexico's southwestern coast. The centre added that Rachel had top sustained winds of 40 mph (65 kph) and was located about 300 miles (485 kilometres) south of Acapulco, Mexico. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect.
